newsitem.title: UK: Soccer stars relax - robot players a distant dream.
newsitem.headline: Soccer stars relax - robot players a distant dream.

text.p: A soccer match staged between robots at a scientific conference on Tuesday drew a sharp line between what machines can achieve on an assembly line and in the realm of human activity.
The urge to create artificial life could be considered to be making some progress, but aspiring soccer stars still seem to have little to fear.

Five robots -- six-cm (2.5-inch) wheeled vehicles, each costing about $4,000 and resembling a big computer chip with a tiny camera on top -- vied to roll a tennis ball into rival goals on a 70 by 90 cm (27.5 by 35.5 inch) pitch.
Three kept getting stuck against a wall, and another scored more than twice as many goals against itself than it did against its opponents.

The match at the conference on artificial life in this southern English seaside resort was an exhibition warm-up before the official launch of a World "RoboCup" next month in Japan in which 45 teams of five robots each will compete.
"This just shows how far we still have to go," said Hiroaki Kitano, senior researcher at Sony Corp in Japan, which will be fielding a team at the tournament.
Now that IBM's Deep Blue computer had defeated the world chess champion, soccer is becoming a new focus for scientists, he said.
The ultimate prize is to develop a side capable of defeating Brazil's World Cup team. But just creating a humanoid that could stand up to human competition is still at least 100 years off, he said.
"In the real world, you cannot break things down as you can in chess. Everything moves around dynamically and things change all the time. There is missing information."
A big stumbling block is simply ensuring that a robot would not harm its human opponents. "Robots must learn when to give up the goal," Kitano said.
A practical application could be robots which were able to fight fires and save victims.
"A robot could go in and pull out a victim, but what happens if it pulls him apart in the process?" Kitano mused.
Aside from the minature soccer players, some robots on display ranged from the freakish to the cute.
One, a do-it-itself cleaner -- an Autonomous Mobile Vehicule -- costs $16,000 minus the vacuum and modifications.

Chris Winter, head of the futures research lab at British Telecom, which sponsored the project, said his company was looking for ways to cut down on software costs. Together with MCI, BT spends more than $2 billion a year on software, he said.
"These people here are developing new ways of thinking about complexity. New ways for the future," he said.
